name: TPS61022RWUR
title: TPS61022: 8-A valley-limit synchronous boost converter, 0.5 V to 5.5 V input, 2 mm × 2 mm VQFN-HR
summary: The TPS61022 is a synchronous step-up converter with both power switches on chip (18 mΩ high side, 12 mΩ low side) and a valley-sensed switch current limit of 8 A typical, 6.5 A minimum. It needs at least 1.8 V on VIN to start, and once its output is above 2.2 V it keeps running with the input as low as 0.5 V; the output is set by a resistor divider from 2.2 V to 5.5 V against a 600 mV reference. It switches at about 1 MHz above 1.5 V input, sliding down to 0.6 MHz as the input falls to 1 V. A MODE pin picks PFM or forced PWM at light load; when the input exceeds the set output it passes the input straight through, and in shutdown the output is cut off from the input. It has output overvoltage (5.7 V), short-circuit and thermal protection, and comes in a 7-pin 2 mm × 2 mm VQFN-HR (RWU).

circuits.title: Typical application circuit
circuits.description: The basic boost: a 1 µH inductor from the input to SW, an input capacitor at VIN, an output capacitor at VOUT and a two-resistor divider from VOUT to FB setting the output. MODE is taken to a PWM or PFM level and EN to an on or off level.

circuits.title: Li-ion battery to 5-V boost converter
circuits.description: One Li-ion cell (2.7 V to 4.35 V) boosted to 5 V at up to 3 A. The divider of 732 kΩ over 100 kΩ puts FB at the 600 mV reference when the output is 5 V; three 22 µF ceramics form the output capacitor and 10 µF bypasses the input. MODE selects PWM or PFM and EN switches the converter on or off.

circuits.title: TPS61022 circuit with feedforward capacitor
circuits.description: The basic boost with C3 across the upper feedback resistor R1. C3 adds a zero and a pole to the loop; its value comes from the chosen zero frequency and R1: C3 = 1 / (2π × fFFZ × R1).

circuits.title: TPS61022 circuit for VIN > 4.8-V application
circuits.description: A USB-type input of 4.75 V to 5.25 V giving a 5.0 V output. Diode D1, anode on VIN and cathode on VOUT, charges the output close to the input before the converter is enabled, and with the output pre-biased above 0.7 V the recommended input range reaches 5.5 V instead of 4.8 V. R1 is 732 kΩ and R2 100 kΩ; C1 is 10 µF and C2 three 22 µF capacitors.
notes: Target output for this input: 5 V to 5.25 V.

operation.text: At moderate and heavy load the converter runs quasi-constant-frequency PWM using adaptive constant on-time with valley current-mode control. A predictor sets the on-time from the ratio of input to output voltage. Each cycle starts with the low-side NMOS on, ramping the inductor current from the input while the output capacitor feeds the load; then the NMOS turns off and the high-side PMOS conducts, delivering inductor energy to the output. The next cycle begins when the falling inductor current reaches the level set by the error amplifier, which compares FB with the internal reference. Loop compensation is internal.
The converter can be enabled once VIN rises above the 1.8 V UVLO threshold. After it has started and the output is above 2.2 V, it keeps working with VIN down to 0.5 V.

With VIN above UVLO and EN above 1.2 V the device starts. While the output is under 0.4 V it charges the output capacitors with about 700 mA; above 0.4 V the available current rises to what a 1 Ω load would draw. Once the output reaches the input voltage it begins switching and the output ramps to its target. From EN high to regulation takes 700 µs typical at VIN = 2.5 V, VOUT = 5 V, 30 µF effective output capacitance and no load. Taking EN below 0.4 V shuts the device down completely and disconnects the output from the input.
About 1 MHz while VIN is above 1.5 V. Between 1.5 V and 1 V the frequency falls gradually to 0.6 MHz, which raises efficiency and allows a higher boost ratio; below 1 V it stays at about 0.6 MHz.

The limit is sensed on the valley of the inductor current, from the voltage across the synchronous rectifier during the off-time. If the inductor current stays above the limit for the whole cycle, the off-time stretches until the current falls to the threshold (frequency foldback). In current limit the output voltage drops as the load keeps rising. The largest continuous output current before current limit is IOUT(CL) = (1 − D) × (ILIM + ½ × ΔIL(P-P)).

When the input is above the set output, the output rises above target. At 101% of the target the converter stops switching and holds the high-side PMOS fully on, so the output equals the input less the drop across the inductor DCR and the PMOS RDS(on). Switching resumes when the output falls under 97% of target, as the input drops or the load grows.
Guards against a wrongly fitted feedback divider. Switching stops when the output exceeds about 5.7 V and restarts once the output is 0.1 V below that threshold.

Below 1.8 V on the output the device starts limiting output current, and the lower the output, the smaller the current. With VOUT shorted to ground and the output under 0.4 V the current is held near 700 mA. When the short is removed the device goes through soft start again.
The device shuts down when the junction exceeds 150 °C and restarts when it cools to about 130 °C.
MODE low selects power-save (PFM) operation; MODE high selects forced PWM.

The switching frequency stays constant down to no load. As the load falls the error amplifier lowers the inductor current until it touches zero during each off-time; the PMOS rectifier is not switched off, so the current reverses and energy flows from output back to input. Light-load efficiency is low, but the fixed frequency avoids audible noise and other effects of a low switching frequency.

As the load drops, the inductor valley current falls to its 150 mA floor and the output rises above its set point. When FB reaches the PFM reference the device switches a few more cycles, because of comparator delay, then stops; the output capacitor carries the load and the output sags. When FB falls below the PFM reference, after the same delay, switching starts again. In PFM the output sits around 1.01 × VOUT_NOM, above the PWM level of VOUT_NOM.

The inductor value, saturation current and DCR are the three figures that matter. Inductance from 0.33 µH to 2.9 µH works with this device. A peak-to-peak ripple under 40% of the average inductor current at full load is the usual aim: a larger inductor lowers ripple, core loss and EMI but slows the load-transient response. The saturation current must be above the calculated peak current.

The output capacitor sets ripple and loop stability. X5R or X7R ceramics are recommended, 10 µF to 50 µF after derating; below that range the loop may become unstable. Ceramic capacitance falls with DC bias, ageing and AC signal, and can lose over half its value at rated voltage, so the voltage rating needs margin. More output capacitance lowers the PWM ripple.

Large duty-cycle jitter, or oscillation seen on VOUT or on the inductor current, points to an unstable loop. A load transient also shows it: a response without ringing usually means a phase margin above 45°. A capacitor across R1 adds a zero and a pole and can raise phase margin; its value is C3 = 1 / (2π × fFFZ × R1).

Multilayer X5R or X7R ceramics, as close to the device as possible; 10 µF covers most designs and more lowers input ripple current. When the supply comes over long leads, a load step can ring the lead inductance against an all-ceramic input, coupling to the output and possibly damaging the part; bulk tantalum or aluminium electrolytic capacitance between the ceramic and the source damps it.
For inputs above 4.8 V a diode from VIN to VOUT pre-biases the output before enable. The recommended input limit is 4.8 V with the output below 0.7 V before start-up and 5.5 V with it above 0.7 V.

The input supply should be well regulated and rated for the current the converter draws at its input and output voltages and load. A source more than a few inches away may need bulk capacitance beside the ceramic bypass, typically a 100 µF tantalum or aluminium electrolytic.

Fast switch edges make layout critical. Keep every trace on SW short and small in area, and put a ground plane under the regulator. The input capacitor sits close to both VIN and GND. The highest-di/dt loop runs from the low-side switch through the high-side switch and output capacitor back to the low-side switch ground, so the output ceramic capacitor must sit right at VOUT and GND to limit overshoot on SW and VOUT.

Keep the junction at 125 °C or below in normal use, with PD(max) = (125 − TA) / RθJA. The three power pads (GND, SW, VOUT) carry heat out of the package; large, thick copper on them and many vias joining top-layer and bottom-layer ground copper near the IC, left free of solder mask, lower the real junction-to-ambient resistance, which depends strongly on the board.
